blocks.x: The show was in the group, it was some insurance company, you know, and they had a little show of their own, I mean, just people who worked for the company, you know, one guy to get up and sing, the other, a couple danced, and some guy, I could hear him talking to the panel, I'd like to play that bass, but I see that guy's left hand, I can't play that bass. So Jeff told him, he says, yeah, you think you can, eh? He says, you right-handed? He says, you go get that bass, you'll see. And he was surprised as hell when I gave him the bass, you know, it was tuned, he could just play for a right-hand hand, yeah, play it backwards, that's all.
Play it backwards, so he didn't have to change the bass bar and everything.

Didn't have to change a thing, it happened this way, my grandfather played all stringed instruments, you see, and when I, when this fella loaned me this bass, my grandfather came over to try to show me how to tune it, and being right-hand never occurred to him to show me, you know, he was an old gentleman at the time, and he didn't think about telling me to change the strings back, he just tuned it up and said, here it is. I just took it that way and started picking on it, see, put on a phonograph record, and I had been playing the bass horn for a while then, and I just went right on to this thing. Now let me tell those boys if anything happens the way I am, they come hollering. I told them all. Which one did you tell?
I told Jeff and Bubby and Nina, all of them together.
Good.
Okay. This is over on St. Peter's Street, we have the machine going.
Yeah, 634 St. Peter, the starving artist shop, I want to get it on the tape.
And this is Dick Allen, Bill, you give your name. Yeah, Bill Russell, and we're interviewing-
Sure would manage your pain. Do you have to talk? No, no, no. Just pick it up. Oh, I see.
You might start when you were born, give your birth date if you don't mind.
I was born October 1st, 1912. Right here in New Orleans, yeah.
Do you remember the neighborhood exactly about where you were?
Yeah, on Danty and Oak, and the house is still there. It's my grandfather's residence.
In Carlton or?
Yeah, in the old Cowan section, yeah. Two blocks off of Cowan Avenue, right on the corner of Oak and Danty.
You mentioned a minute ago your grandfather played music?
Oh yeah, he was accomplished on just about all the string instruments. Played the guitar, banjo, bass, and his specialty was violin.
Yeah.
And he was the one that taught me how to tune this instrument and helped me to learn some of the basic things about it.
When did you start in music?

I was about 10 years old, I think, when I started to play. Did you start on the horn or something? No, drums. Drums? Yeah, I was a drummer for maybe three or four years. And then in high school, I just had a desire to play a bass. And there was a bass available there in the school, belonging to the school. And there was an old gentleman named Emil Tasso, who was formerly to conduct at the Orphium Theatre. And when they abandoned the stage shows, vaudeville, well naturally the orchestras were let out, you see. And then those men had to seek employment elsewhere. Yeah. So he got a job as instructor, at that time was Samuel J. Peters, boys high schooler. And I was a student there and I just worked up enough nerve to ask him to loan me that little instrument. And he took it upon himself to let me take it home. And I just played around with it until I got some sounds out of it. And in a couple of weeks I was out playing jobs with his little orchestra in the neighborhood, you see. And then later on, I was playing with a fellow by the name of Joe Klessy. He's well known to all the old timers around here.
Is that the fellow composed some of those numbers?
No, no, I think you have in mind a man composed, I'm sorry I made you cry. What's his name?
N.J. Nick. Nick Klessy, I think.

Nick Klessy, I think. I think he was a realtor. I couldn't say. I don't know. But anyhow, Joe Klessy was the type of guy that would give you the shirt off his back. And he said to me one night, I was playing sousaphone then, only the sousaphone, he said, Why don't you get a string bass? Well in those days you'd play all night for three bucks, you know, and nobody could afford two or three instruments. I was paying for a bass on at the time and I told him, Well I can't afford that. And I don't know if I'd have the coordination never having tried it, you know. I said, It takes some coordination to play a string bass. So, he said, I have one. Come get it and take it home, keep it as long as you want. He was playing drums at the time. So I took the bass home and like I told you before, my grandfather came over and showed me how to tune it. And then I just went on from there with it.
Did you start bowing on it or picking?
No, just the picking, that's all. I never was accomplished with the bow at all.
Did you ever take any formal lessons?
No, Mr. Tasso tried to teach me but I never could get my heart to learn the music, you know. I just wanted to play music and play jazz and that was about it, you know.
By the way, about your grandfather, what kind of music did he play?

Well, to the best of my knowledge, he liked such things as Viennese waltzes, German music, you know. He was an old German gentleman and he told me that it was a custom when he was a young man to go around and serenade the girls. You know, they'd go around and play outside the house and somebody would generally come out and give them a, well some kind of refreshments, maybe liquid or otherwise, you know. Yeah. Sometime they'd give them a shower bath, they'd toss something down on them and run them up the street too.
Just a string group of triors?
Yeah, he said they'd walk around with maybe a guitar, a banjo and a violin, something like that, you see.
And about Joe Clancy, how many instruments did he play?
That I know of, bass, trombone and drums. Now if there were any others I don't know. I know he had those instruments and I saw him play them.
Do you remember any other music? Did you hear any of those string trios around serenading when you were a boy?
No, I don't remember. I think it was a little before I, uh, was aware of music. I mean, as I know it today, you know, I really cared a lot about the music.
Do you remember any parades when you were a boy hearing?

Oh yeah. Oh, I hope to tell you. I remember the funerals too. The colored bands, you know, marching and playing those mournful duvages, you know, on the way to the cemetery and then coming back, man, they'd be knocking it out, you know, swinging.
Do you remember which bands they were? The name of any other?
No, but I think I remember seeing Celestine. He's one of the first fellas that I can remember seeing and identifying with bands, as well as a man by the name of Ridgely.
Yeah, he's still living up there.

Ridgely, uh, last time I saw him was crippled. He must have had a stroke or something. And, uh, I remembered him. Of course, he didn't remember me. I was just a fan, you know. I used to, my father used to take me to ball games on Sunday morning. They were ball games at the old ballpark here, Heinemann Park it was. And he'd take my second brother and I and just let us in the vicinity of the band, you see. They'd have this band playing. It was a tuxedo. And we would sit there and he could roam all over that park. When he came back, he knew where to find us. We would be right by that band. And the same thing goes for the steam of capital. And there may have been other boats that I don't remember the names of, but, uh, Faint Marables band was playing. And I remember my mother and father used to go on there and go on to dance. You know, they appreciated the music too, but I was... Did the radio mothers play anything? No, no. My mother, but not my father. My mother was a pianist. But they would take us on the boat. We were small children and they could just put us by the band, you know. And we were there all night just listening and watching these fellas play. And I remember... And the super time of old years then? Yeah, I remember Faint Marable very well. And, uh, I can remember Red Allen. And I think Louie was a little before me on that boat. I remember he... I remember reading of him being on the boat, but I don't think I ever saw Louie because I would have remembered him. And the other fellas I don't remember. But I remember Red, Allen, and, uh, Faint.
I know you've told me that you collect the Armstrong records.
Oh, yeah, and I've had...
That's a wonderful collection.
I got several from you. Several fine ones that I didn't have that you were kind enough to let me have, and I still have.
When did you start collecting those records?

Well, as I can remember, I think Louie's the only one that I ever listened to. I heard the other ones, but I just... Louie's the only one I ever paid any serious attention to. And I was... I guess I was nine or ten years old. I don't know. It's to the best of my recollection around that time. I would...
Who were some of the bass players that you liked when you were a boy? Do you remember some of them here?
No, I can't remember any of them. No, I can't. There were... Well, wait now. I remember... Seems like I remember Frank Netto. I think I remember Frank playing in the Two Bits Club. Yeah, it cost me.
Yeah, okay. I was wondering, you told me once before about Pops Foster, that you'd heard him on the record. You...

Well, I heard him, and my only recollection of him is being with Louie. I identify him with Armstrong's band, with the Louie Russell band. I remember having seen him here at different spots in New Orleans. At the Coliseum for one place. And other places, the names of which I can't recall at the moment.
Sure. What about early dance bands? Can you remember the very first dance music?

I can remember bands like the Owls. Of course, I was a little boy, and I wasn't able to go to the dance, but I can remember hearing records. And then it was the early days of radio. I can remember I had a little crystal set, and I used to sit down and tune in. And of course, I was looking for the music, and nothing else interested me. I wanted to hear the music. There were some good bands, and I think... Oh, no, let me see. I mentioned the Owls. I don't know. I can't remember the others. But I can remember bands like the New Orleans Rhythm Kings on records, and the Halfway House Orchestra, Johnny Byersdorfer. And then I'll have to always go back to Louie, you know, his records, those early records, those wonderful records, and I have a lot of them home. I spend a lot of my time listening to them, I'll tell you. Especially today when you don't have nothing but this rock and roll.
Who was in Classy's band, by the way?

Oh, he had a fine old bass player. Strictly a faker, as I remember it, but boy, he could play. Philly Miller was his name. Philly? Miller. His father was a one-man band runner. He used to be on Canal Street. Oh, yeah. He used to go around and had a little outfit of drums and a kazoo, a banjo. And he played everything imaginable, you know, with his hands and feet, all at one time.
I saw him down by the ferry, that's a guy.

And another one in the family, you may have seen around the front, that's a little fella. Played with him. Lost his legs. Oh, yeah? Yeah, he had a little platform he would ride. I used to see him around the famous door when I was playing there on Sundays and Mondays.
Why do your outsiders keep putting the answers in our mouth? Let Bill talk.
Oh, yeah.
I was wondering about some of the early bands that you played with, some of the very first bands that you mentioned.

Well, the first one that I remember was a little group that we had. My second brother was a saxophone player at the time, and we had a little trio. We had a, I played the drum at the time, my brother played the saxophone, and we had a boy with a banjo. He later went over the piano and we got another boy on the banjo. And we used to play for all the little functions in those days, like weddings, king parties, birthday parties. And it was customary then to have those parties in the homes, in the private residences. Today, it seems everybody has to go to hotels and places that specialize in such things as that, you see. But in those days, a small combination like we had was adequate for a party in a residence, because the places weren't too big and three or four pieces sufficed.
About how old were you when you got paid for your first job? Do you remember?
Ten or eleven years old. And my brother was about, well, he would be eight or nine, because it was three years difference in this particular brother and myself.
You were still playing tuba then? Or the strings? No, no, just the drums.
Oh, the drums. Yeah, yeah. I started on this little bass horn, and I went to high school. I guess I was about fourteen then, something like that.
And when you took up your string bass, which band did you belong to first?
Classy. Same thing? I was playing with Classy when he loaned me that bass, and I started to play the thing in his band.
Do you remember some of the jobs you played in different places, aside from parties?

Well, I remember playing at the Woodman of the World Hall, a place called Circle. It was an open-air place. We played there four nights a week. Dutch Andrus' band. And I played on the boat a lot with Dutch. And I used to go over and play in Covington. There was a boat that used to operate from New Orleans to Madisonville. And the name of the boat was in Madisonville. And I think at the same time there was one in operation by the name of the Susquehanna. And we had...
Remember the Camellia, too? Was there one called the Camellia? Was that the same?

I seem to recall that, but not in the same connection. I think that was a boat that was rented out for parties. I think they used to rent it out for parties. Seeming as if it was a yacht. Now, I might be wrong, but it seemed like it was a... The Camellia was a yacht, but I stand to be corrected on that point. But we used to go to Covington to play for private parties. People would hire us to come over. And as soon as we'd get on the boat, we'd start playing. Just out of goodness of our hearts and for the love of it. We didn't expect any money. We didn't get any. The only money we got was when we got to Covington and played. These people would meet us at Madisonville rather than take us to Covington in their automobile. And we'd play our job and stay at their home. And next day we'd get the boat and come back to New Orleans. Is there dancing on the boat? Oh yeah. As soon as we unpacked those instruments, there was dancing. And on the way back, it'd be a repeat performance.
So, you mentioned some kind of king party or something?

Yeah, it's some custom they have here. And it might be elsewhere, but as I know it, it's in New Orleans. It's a party that the kids have. You know, they buy these cakes at the bakeries. And there's a little doll. Some kind of little china doll thing in the cake, baked in the cake. And then they slice the cake up and whoever finds that, either in his hand or in his mouth, is obligated to give the next party. You know, provide the refreshments and entertainment and the sight.
Oh. He's deaf, you know. Oh yeah. Oh, I see.
Well now, what were the other kind of parties you mentioned? And what did they consist of? What kind of customs?

Well, I think a lot of those parties were little private parties, just things that people gave just for the fun of it, you know. And I can remember also playing for the mayor of the city. And we were so small. In those days, the little boys wore short pants, not like today. As soon as they can walk around, they'd give them a pair of long pants. We had long black stockings and little short pants. And we couldn't get around because we had no transportation. And my mother wouldn't let us go out and play unless whoever hired us to play would agree to come and pick us up and bring us back home. Because there was no such thing as little boys roaming the streets at 12 and 1 o'clock in the morning, you know. And Mr. O'Keefe, the mayor, would send his son to my house. And they would pick us up and take us to wherever this party would be in and bring us back after. And in those days, the parties they gave were mainly stags. And not like we know stags today. In those days, we were just eating and drinking. That's all. A bunch of men, no entertainment other than a little musical aggregation. And then the main course, the spaghetti and the wine, the chicken and what have you.
I think you told me before when I interviewed you without the recorder that Pops Foster influenced your style.

Oh yeah. Oh yeah. Always admired his playing. And I think some of the classic examples of his playing is in the Armstrong Band, which of course I think was actually the Louis Russell Band, but Armstrong fronted the band. Those records like Swing That Music, where his slapping really stands out. And well, some of the fine tunes like this tune Louis composed, If We Never Meet Again. I mean, his bass just influenced me. I always listened for it and did whatever I could to try to sound like Pops Foster.
Were you able to get that from the record, most of it?
Yeah. Yeah. Even though it wasn't reproduced as faithfully as it is today. And we didn't have to find instruments like the hi-fi sets and stereo, but you could still hear him. He was hood, all right.
Yeah. Did you remember many other people playing that style here, of slapping the bass?

No. I remember hearing Tom Brown's brother. He was with Gene Goldcat. But I didn't know who he was at the time. I only had the pleasure of meeting him within the last few years, when I became associated with Tom Brown through the New Orleans Jazz Club. And not many years before Tom passed away, his brother visited here, and then I was able to meet him. Yeah. He played that same style. He played that style. And he was given credit, I think, for being a man that started that. Yes. In fact, I read that in a publication of the International Musicians.
I remember Tom showed us that article.
Yeah. I think they made some award to his brother. Yeah. In recognition of his starting that slapping on the bass.
But you never heard him in person in the old days down here?
Never did. No. No.
You were too young.

That's right. But not too much, though, because I remember it was here. I think he was with the Rhythm Kings. Is that correct? In Chicago? He played here before. And I have only one of their records, I think. And maybe I should have more. But I have She's Crying For Me Blues. And on the other side, I think, is Maple Leaf Strut. Is that right? Or Maple Leaf Rag. Oh, Golden Leaf. Golden Leaf Strut. That's right. Mm-hmm.
Who are your favorite bass players today, would you say?

Yeah. Yeah. Marty Cobb. Bob Haggart. Bob Haggart especially, I think. And there's some colored bass players in New York. One of them with this band, the Paris Brothers. I can't tell you the man's name, but he comes through pretty good on that, too, I think.
Yeah, I can't tell you.
I think he provides a good beat in that band, together with the drum and the banjo.
When you work in a band, what kind of a rhythm section do you like to have? Piano, guitar, bass, or banjo? What are your favorites? I like a banjo.

Like a banjo. Of course, I get along well with the guitar players, but I like to hear a banjo. I like that nice, clean beat that it provides and the way it cuts through the rhythm section. You know, it can be heard well and it's very pronounced.
Did you ever work with the old bands before they used piano all the time?

No, I can't recall that. Except these little groups I told you I played with as a child. There wasn't many piano players available, you know. They just weren't around and not too many people had the pianos to begin with. Yeah, that's right. You had to depend on some other instrument, the banjo or the guitar, you know, for your rhythm, with your drum and your bass.
Did you ever get in on the days when they'd advertise on a truck?

Oh, I played on some of those things. Of course, I think that was toward the end of those days, but I remember playing on trucks, advertising dances and such things as that, you know. I think I even played on a wagon on one or two occasions, yeah.
Ever play any parades in a brass band with your drum?

Yeah, I certainly did. I remember one carnival day we played for an organization from across the river, not a well-known organization, but they needed a band, we needed a job, so we played it. And in the hot sun, and before the thing started, they passed out the spirit, you see. I wish I never saw it before that parade was over. I guess we marched 30 miles and me counting a big sousaphone in that boiling sun, and liquor trying to get out the best way it could. Boy, boy, boy.
What kind of music would you play in the brass bands? Would it be straight marches?

We used to play jazz. That's all. And the people seemed to like it. We didn't play too much marching music. I mean, we knew jazz, we thought we did, and we played it the way we knew it, you know, just rip it off.
Who would lead those brass bands? Do you remember?

Well, a lot of times it would be just men they would pick up and put together, you know. It was no organized group that I played with. It would just be a bunch of men with blue horns, you know, and you just get an end blow.
What were some of your other favorite bands during the early days that you heard in person? Do you remember any of them?

Well, I remember going to some of these dance halls around here, like the Fuen. And I can remember fellas like Buzzy Willows, he's dead. Farzola. I played with Farzola, he was a little boy too. He was in Short Pass too. We played some jobs together. And I had to Woodman Hall. And I played one job with Sidney Aridon. The fella that was co-composer with Hoagie Carmichael, I think, on Lazy River. One time, that's all I remember was Sidney Aridon. After he came back from wherever he went away from me, I guess up north, and he came back. Did he seem exceptional? Oh yeah, he was a standout. Yeah, he was a standout. You could recognize a man like that. Oh yeah. What did Buzzy Willows play? Buzzy played guitar and banjo. And he sang some. He was a fine rhythm man though. But he passed away at an early age. We were playing on a job, I think it was that circle job I told you about before. Four nights a week and he died in his automobile. Died at the wheel. Yeah.
What style would he play? Would he play just a straight four?

Yeah. Yeah. No, no, no. Those early bands, I don't remember them playing shuffle rhythm. The only one, the first band I remember playing shuffle rhythm was this trumpet player. Oh man. What is his name? Any of you gentlemen remember? Here in town? No, no, it was a nationally known orchestra. Henry Bussey? Henry Bussey. That's the first shuffle rhythm I can recall. Henry Bussey seemed to be the one to produce that. And these guys down here would play four or two of them? Oh, they'd just play a beat, man. Four beats. I mean, on a banjo or a string instrument in the rhythm section. They seemed to play that four beats.
When would they play two beats? If ever?

Well, I don't recall that. I don't recall. I'm trying to associate that beat with some of the tunes that I think about and I just can't. I can remember them just a nice flowing easy beat, four beats, you know. How fast? Well, naturally, it'd depend on the tempo. They'd change. You know, I mean, we'd play some tunes slow, some tunes would be medium, and then we'd play some pretty fast ones at times.
Did they play as fast then as they do today?

I think some of the tunes they did, like we associate a speedy tempo with Tiger Rag. Well, they played pretty well up in those days, too. I get a kick out of Lewis, some of those tempos he plays Tiger Rag. I think I have three or four records, the Masters, you know, that he made, and they all really going. Now, those...
What else do they play? Do they play waltzes or anything on your own?

Oh yeah, yeah, yeah. I always go back and remember the pretty tunes, you know. I always loved ballads and pretty waltzes as well as these jazz tunes, you see. I just get a lot of kick out of playing all of them. I love the jazz first, but I also like to play ballads and pretty waltzes. In those days, I think the emphasis was on that. I mean, they knew a lot about pretty music, and they knew how to play it, too. Of course, these bands, like in these two-bits clubs they used to have around here, those fellas could really play that jazz, clarinet, marmalade, and baratarian, oh man. All those old tunes, those fine old tunes. We had them all on record, and somehow through the years they slipped away. Like the Halfway House Band, I think they made a lot of fine records, and... I don't know, in those days there's so many good ones. New Orleans Rhythm, Kings, and I should have more of their records, but I do not have one.
Do you remember hearing the Brunus Brothers around here?
I remember hearing them on the records, but I was too small to go into clubs then, you see.
Did you ever work on Bourbon Street yourself here?

Once. I had one job, and it lasted about a year, at the Famous Door. Two nights a week, a jazz trio. We used to relieve... At that time, George Girard was one of the bands, and the Dukes of Dixieland was the other band at the Famous Door, and the union demanded, of course, they get a night off. Sure. And that would be a Sunday and a Monday, you see. So, when those bands were off, the club provided entertainment in the form of this jazz trio. And I was a member of that trio. It was Jeff Riddick, Raymond Boyk, and myself. And we would play at the intermissions when the six-piece band would be off at a stand, and we'd get up and play for twenty minutes out of an hour. And our biggest problem was trying to find something to do with ourselves, and at forty minutes, you know, we'd just have to sit there and listen to the other bands. Okay.
I guess we'd better... Yeah. I guess we'd better... Yeah. I guess we'd better... Yeah.
You can go ahead, too.
Okay.
Well, it was sure nice talking to y'all. I'll see you later. Thank you. Thank you. I'll see you later. We have something to tell you. Oh, forget about it.
I'll see you. We'll make a note here that this was made over here on St. Peter's Street tonight. The Coca-Cola TV program was being filmed. Yeah. Anything else to add, Dick?
No.
If you heard somebody yelling out on the street, it's the director of the TV production, I guess. .

segments.title: Playing a right-handed bass backwards after his grandfather tuned it
segments.summary: Sherwood explains that his grandfather tuned the borrowed bass for a right-handed player, so he plays it backwards and a left-handed would-be player can use it.

segments.title: Recording setup on St. Peter Street
segments.summary: Names of friends told, the location (634 St. Peter, starving artist shop) and the interviewers are noted for the tape.

segments.title: Born in 1912 at his grandfather's house, a string player
segments.summary: Born October 1, 1912 at Danty and Oak in New Orleans, his grandfather's house; the grandfather played guitar, banjo, bass and violin and taught him to tune.

segments.title: Starting on drums, then borrowing the school bass from Emil Tasso
segments.summary: He began on drums at about ten, then took up the bass at high school, borrowing the school instrument from Emil Tasso, and soon played neighborhood jobs.

segments.title: Joe Klessy gives him a string bass
segments.summary: After a mix-up with composer Nick Klessy, Sherwood describes bandleader Joe Klessy, who lent him a string bass when he was playing sousaphone.

segments.title: Picking, never bowing, and no formal lessons
segments.summary: He only picked the bass, never mastered the bow, and Tasso's attempts to teach him music failed.

segments.title: Grandfather's German serenading music
segments.summary: His grandfather liked Viennese waltzes and German music and told of serenading girls with guitar, banjo and violin.

segments.title: Instruments Joe Clancy played
segments.summary: Joe Clancy played bass, trombone and drums as far as Sherwood knows.

segments.title: Boyhood parades and funeral bands, Celestin and Ridgely
segments.summary: He remembers colored funeral bands playing dirges and then swinging, and recalls Celestin and Ridgely as the first bandleaders he identified.

segments.title: Heinemann Park bands and the riverboat with Fate Marable
segments.summary: His father left the boys by the band at ball games, and his parents took them on the steamer to hear Fate Marable's band, with Red Allen recalled.

segments.title: Collecting Louis Armstrong records
segments.summary: Armstrong is the only musician he paid serious attention to, from about age nine or ten, and Bill Russell gave him several records.

segments.title: Boyhood bass players: Frank Netto and Pops Foster
segments.summary: He recalls Frank Netto in a club and identifies Pops Foster with the Armstrong and Luis Russell band, seen at the Coliseum.

segments.title: Early dance bands, crystal set radio and records
segments.summary: He heard the Owls, the New Orleans Rhythm Kings and the Halfway House Orchestra on records and radio, and always returns to early Armstrong.

segments.title: Philly Miller and his one-man-band father
segments.summary: In Classy's band the bass player was Philly Miller, whose father was a Canal Street one-man band; another relative lost his legs.

segments.title: First bands: the family trio and Classy's band
segments.summary: His first band was a trio with his saxophone-playing brother for house parties, paid at ten or eleven; he first played string bass in Classy's band.

segments.title: Dutch Andrus, Circle hall and the Covington boat
segments.summary: He played with Dutch Andrus at Woodman of the World Hall and on the boat to Madisonville and Covington for private parties.

segments.title: King parties, stag parties and playing for the mayor
segments.summary: He explains the king cake custom and recalls playing as boys for private parties and stags, picked up by the mayor's son.

segments.title: Pops Foster's influence on his style
segments.summary: He admired Pops Foster's slap bass on Armstrong band records and tried to sound like him.

segments.title: Tom Brown's brother and the origin of slap bass
segments.summary: He remembers Tom Brown's brother, with Goldkette, as credited with starting slap bass, and owns one Rhythm Kings record.

segments.title: Favorite bass players today
segments.summary: He names Bob Haggart and a bass player in a New York band as favorites.

segments.title: Preferred rhythm section and early piano-less groups
segments.summary: He likes banjo for its clean beat, and says early groups used banjo or guitar because pianos were scarce.

segments.title: Advertising trucks and brass band parades
segments.summary: He played on advertising trucks and in pickup brass bands that played jazz, including a hot carnival parade.

segments.title: Dance halls, Buzzy Willows and Sidney Arodin
segments.summary: He recalls dance halls, guitarist Buzzy Willows who died at the wheel, and one job with Sidney Arodin.

segments.title: Four-beat rhythm, shuffle rhythm and tempos
segments.summary: Early bands played four beats; the first shuffle rhythm he recalls was Henry Busse; tempos could be fast like Tiger Rag.

segments.title: Ballads, waltzes and the old jazz repertoire on record
segments.summary: He loved jazz first but also ballads and waltzes, and recalls two-bit club tunes and records of the Halfway House and NORK.

segments.title: Jazz trio at the Famous Door on Bourbon Street
segments.summary: He played about a year, two nights a week, in a trio with Jeff Riddick and Raymond Boyk relieving the Girard and Dukes of Dixieland bands.

segments.title: Goodbyes and note about the TV filming
segments.summary: The interview wraps up with a note that it was made on St. Peter Street during a TV filming.
